title: Planning care for bilingual dementia? A family message in her own language is easy to collect and safe to play.
meta_title: Bilingual Dementia: A Family Message in Her Language | CareStreamAI
meta_description: A relative records a message in her first language. You read the automatic English translation, check it and approve. Staff play it.
lede: A resident who has spoken two languages all her life may find English tiring, and her family know the words and the voice that feel like home. Teams working with bilingual dementia often ask how a relative can send a message in that language, and how a manager can know what it says. CareStream gives them a private link, translates the speech for you to read before you approve, and lets staff play it. It sits alongside your training and policy tools.

intro.heading: She came to England at nineteen. She still counts in Polish.
intro.sub: A scenario we see in many care settings.
intro.paragraph: Mrs Nowak came from Kraków as a young woman and worked in a Bolton mill. Her English is good, but in the evenings the team hear her speaking Polish to nobody in particular. Nobody on shift speaks it. Her grandson, Tomasz, lives in Leeds and says he could record a few minutes of her favourite sayings and a bread recipe. The manager, Rukhsana, likes the idea, and wants it checked, kept private, and findable by a carer who has never met her.

trail.text: The home records that Mrs Nowak speaks Polish and English.
Her key worker learns three Polish greetings.
Tomasz offers to record a message in Polish.
There is no safe way to receive it. The offer fades.
She speaks Polish more in the evenings. Staff cannot answer her.
Tomasz sends a clip to a carer's phone. It has to be deleted.
Nobody is sure what to play, or what it says.
“How do you meet her communication needs?” You have three greetings.

trail_close: The family could give her something in her own language. The gap is between that and a safe way to use it. Here is how CareStream collects a message, shows you what it says, lets you check it, and lets any carer find it.

why.heading: Language is part of who a person is
why.sub: Staff do not need to understand every word to offer a familiar voice.

cards.title: A familiar voice, in her own words
cards.body: Families of people with bilingual dementia often tell us that the first language feels like home. Staff may not share it, but a grandson speaking it gives a carer a name and a voice to sit beside. We make no claim about what it does for any person.

cards.title: Care should reflect the person
cards.body: Care must meet a person's needs and reflect their preferences. Where someone cannot decide for themselves, the Mental Capacity Act asks you to consider their past and present wishes and feelings, and to consult people interested in their welfare where practicable and appropriate.

cards.title: A message you cannot read still needs checking
cards.body: A clip in another language can still show other people or say something the resident would not want played. CareStream turns the speech into text and an English translation for you to read, but a manager still has to approve it. Regulation 10 includes ensuring the privacy of the person.

how.heading: From a private link to a message any carer can play.
how.sub: Video messages are part of the resident profiles feature, in the same system as your policies and training. They are on Professional and above. See how staff use resident knowledge too.

blocks.heading: The family record in whichever language they choose
bullets: You invite the relative by name and email from the resident's record. They get a private link, with no account. What they record is up to them, in any language
They tap Record a message, which opens the phone camera, or Choose a video. Each clip can be up to 60 seconds, with up to 5 on one link and up to 150MB per upload

They can add a short title of up to 60 characters and remove a clip before pressing Send. A line above the buttons asks them to share only what they are happy for the care team to play, and says that speech in another language is turned into text and translated so a manager can understand it

blocks.heading: You read what is said, check it, and approve
bullets: The video waits on the Approvals tab. Play it there. A What is said panel shows the language, the original words and an English translation, marked Machine generated
Check anything important with someone who speaks the language. If the translation is off, choose Edit translation. Edits record who made them
You can tick the box to show the English text to staff, then choose Approve or Reject. Rejecting removes the video and its words at once

English translation: Good morning, Babcia. I made your bread today.
Show the English text to staff when this video is played

blocks.heading: Staff find it by the title and note, then press play
bullets: In the This is me chat a carer asks, for example, “do we have a message in Polish?”. The chat finds videos by the approved title and note only, and the video appears with the resident's name and room number
A Messages from family button lists a person's approved videos, newest first. Playing opens just the video on a dimmed backdrop. If you ticked the box, the English text appears under it
Each play is logged with who and when. The assistant never watches a video or uses the words

talk.heading: The questions managers ask, and how CareStream answers them
talk.sub: Read this as a conversation. The questions are the ones we hear most.

items.q: A grandson wants to record a message in Polish. Can he?
items.a: Yes. You invite him from the resident's record, and on his private link he records a short video in any language. A line tells him the speech is turned into text and translated for a manager. Nothing reaches your team until you approve it.

items.q: Staff do not speak the language. Does that matter?
items.a: Not for playing it. A carer finds the video from its title and note and presses play. If you tick the box, staff also see the English translation under the video, labelled as machine generated and checked by a manager.

Yes, for you as the manager. The speech is turned into text and translated into English automatically, and you read it on the Approvals screen before you approve. It is not subtitles and it is not live.

items.q: How do I check a video I cannot understand?
items.a: Read the What is said panel: language, original words and English translation. It is machine generated and can be wrong, so check anything important with someone who speaks the language, and edit the translation if needed. You are the approver.

items.q: Will it help with dementia confusion?
items.a: We would not say that. CareStream does not treat or change anything. It gives staff a personal message to play, safely. How you use it with each person is for you and your team to judge.

items.q: Can the assistant use what is said in it?
items.a: No. It never watches a video or uses the words or the translation. The chat still finds videos by the title and note you approve, so write those clearly.

items.q: What happens if the resident moves on?
items.a: Their videos leave the hub straight away, and any still waiting are deleted with their words. Approved files and their words stay in private storage for the retention period, like the written profile, then are deleted with it.

items.q: Which plan is it on, and can I try it?
items.a: Resident profiles, videos and the translation are on Professional and above. There is a 14 day free trial. You can create an account or book a demo, and the pricing page has the plan details.

limits.heading: Honest limits: the translation helps you check, it does not replace a person

cards.title: Machine generated, and it can be wrong
cards.body: The translation is automatic. It may miss words or feeling, and not every language it can recognise is guaranteed to translate well. Welsh is not supported. Check anything important with someone who speaks the language.

cards.title: Not subtitles, not live, not on by default
cards.body: Nothing is added to the video. Staff see the English text only if you tick the box. The chat finds videos by title and note, not by what is said.

cards.title: It is a message, not a conversation
cards.body: The family record once and the team plays it back. No video calls, no reply from the resident, and no claim about dementia confusion.

faqs.heading: Messages in a first language, answered

items.q: What are some dementia communication tips for a resident whose first language is not English?
items.a: Ask the family which words, phrases and names matter, and write them into the profile. Learn a few greetings, use a calm tone, and offer familiar things such as a recording. Read more in our guide to the this is me document.

items.q: How does a family message fit with bilingual dementia care?
items.a: It is one personal item among many. Teams caring for someone with bilingual dementia often record the languages they use and when, then add a voice the person knows. We make no claim about outcomes.

items.q: Does the system watch the video or describe it?
items.a: The assistant does not. It never watches or describes a video and never uses the words. The system does turn the speech into text and an English translation for the manager to read. It is machine generated and can be wrong.

items.q: Which languages can it read and translate?
items.a: English (UK and US), Arabic, Bengali, Chinese, French, Gujarati, Hindi, Italian, Polish, Portuguese, Punjabi, Romanian, Spanish, Tamil and Urdu. Welsh is not supported. If the language is not supported, you see the original text only, with a message.

items.q: How long can a family video be?
items.a: Up to 60 seconds each, up to 5 on one link, and up to 150MB per upload. The family can add a title of up to 60 characters and remove a clip before pressing Send.

items.q: Does a manager have to approve every video?
items.a: Yes. A family video stays hidden from staff until you approve it. You can edit the title and add a note first, or reject it. Videos you add yourself are approved at once.

items.q: Who can see the words and the translation?
items.a: Only managers and admins, unless you tick the box for that video. They are deleted with the video, whether it is rejected, deleted or the profile is removed.

guide.heading: How to use a first language message well
guide.lede: A few habits make the difference between a clip nobody can find and one that helps at the right moment. Ask for a short message, read the translation, write a clear English title, and check before you approve.

sections.h3: Ask the family for a short, warm message
paragraphs: Tell the relative that 30 or 40 seconds is plenty. A greeting, the person's name and one small story is enough. Ask them to put a title on it that says who it is from. Short, clear speech also gives the automatic translation its best chance.

Watch it as a new carer would, then read the What is said panel. The translation is machine generated, so check anything important with someone who speaks the language. Write the title and note in English so staff can find it. Reject anything that shows other people who might not want it shared. See dignity and respect in regulation 10.
checklist: Is the speaker someone the resident would be glad to hear?
Does the translation make sense, and has someone who speaks the language checked anything important?
Does it show anyone else who might not want it shared?
Do you want staff to see the English text under the video?

sections.h3: Record the language in the profile too
paragraphs: A message does not replace knowing the person. Note which languages she uses and when. The dementia awareness course helps staff see why this matters.
